# Continuity walkthrough

A step-through visualization of the protocol, for hosting on GitHub Pages or
embedding in a post.

* **`index.html`** — the page. Loads `scenarios.json` at startup, so it needs to
  be served over HTTP rather than opened from disk.
* **`scenarios.json`** — the traces, generated by the test suite.

```bash
cd Visualization
python3 -m http.server
```

## Where the runs come from

Nobody chose these interleavings. Each scenario in `../Spec/Scenarios.cs`
states only the **shape** of the run it is about — the conditions it must pass
through, in order — and the model supplies a run that does it. Regenerate them
by running the test suite:

```bash
dotnet test src/Continuity.csproj
```

The suite writes `scenarios.json` as its last step, so the page can never show a
run the protocol does not have.

A scenario may name a `group`, and the page draws one row per group in the
order the groups first appear. The list is not fixed anywhere: naming a new
group in the spec adds a row, and naming none puts the scenario in an
unlabelled row.

Three shapes turn out to be **impossible**, which is the protocol working
rather than a gap in the scenarios: no read is ever served at a position
longer than the repository behind it, no two reads at the same position
return different repositories, and no packfile is left uploaded-but-
uncommitted once everything has settled.

## Two views of the same run

**State** is the state as the checker holds it, one `path = value` line per
field, with the fields this step changed marked and the previous value struck
through beside them. It knows nothing about Continuity — it flattens whatever
the export contains — so it is also the view that shows a step doing *nothing*,
which really happens here: a second read served at the same position adds
nothing to `readsServed`, because that field is a set.

**Visual** is the protocol-specific picture: replicas on the left, the object
store on the right, and between them the request this step made. Each replica
shows **its own cached copy of the index**, which is what makes a race legible —
two replicas claiming the same position while the store's copy has neither.

## What the export carries, and what it does not

`scenarios.json` is the model and nothing else: each frame is a state the
checker produced, plus the `action` and `label` of the step that produced it.
The action is the enum as declared; the label names the instance — usually just
the replica, and `r1-start`, `r1-rebase` or `r1-refresh` for the three steps
that share the action `ReadIndex` and differ only in their guard.

Every sentence on screen is written in `index.html`, derived from those states.
Whether a compare-and-swap won is read from whether the stored version moved;
whether a replica is stale, from whether the index it holds is the stored one;
the log position an index describes, from the entries it names. None of that is
in the JSON, and none of it is in the C#.

That line is deliberate. The exporter can stay ignorant of how the protocol is
explained, the page can be rewritten without touching the model, and the same
export drives a view that does not know what a replica is.

## Hosting

The directory is self-contained. Point Pages at it, or copy `index.html` and
`scenarios.json` somewhere that serves both from the same path.
